latest_nl_proof:
Let deg_q denote the degree of a nonzero rational function in q: if F(q)=P(q)/Q(q) with P,Q in Q[q] both nonzero, define deg_q(F):=deg P-deg Q. This is well defined, because if P/Q=P'/Q' as rational functions, then PQ'=P'Q, so deg P+deg Q'=deg P'+deg Q, hence deg P-deg Q=deg P'-deg Q. Also, for nonzero rational functions F and G, one has deg_q(FG)=deg_q(F)+deg_q(G).

We first compute the degree of [n choose a]_q.

If a=0, then by the empty-product convention [n choose 0]_q=1, so deg_q([n choose 0]_q)=0=0(n-0).

Now assume 1<=a<=n. For each i=1,2,...,a, set
F_i(q):=(1-q^(n-a+i))/(1-q^i).
Because a<=n, we have n-a+i>=1, and of course i>=1; thus both 1-q^(n-a+i) and 1-q^i are nonzero polynomials. Therefore

deg_q(F_i)=deg(1-q^(n-a+i)) - deg(1-q^i) = (n-a+i)-i = n-a.

Using multiplicativity of degree for nonzero rational functions,

deg_q([n choose a]_q)
= deg_q(prod_{i=1}^a F_i(q))
= sum_{i=1}^a deg_q(F_i)
= sum_{i=1}^a (n-a)
= a(n-a).

This proves the first claim.

Now assume 0<=a<b<=n/2. Since each factor (1-q^(n-t+i))/(1-q^i) is a nonzero rational function, both [n choose a]_q and [n choose b]_q are nonzero; hence their quotient is also nonzero. Its degree is

deg_q(([n choose a]_q)/([n choose b]_q))
= deg_q([n choose a]_q)-deg_q([n choose b]_q)
= a(n-a)-b(n-b).

A simple factorization gives

a(n-a)-b(n-b)=(a-b)(n-a-b).

Here a-b<0 because a<b. Also, from a<b<=n/2 we get a+b<2b<=n, so n-a-b>0. Hence

deg_q(([n choose a]_q)/([n choose b]_q))=(a-b)(n-a-b)<0.

Therefore the rational function [n choose a]_q/[n choose b]_q has negative degree.

Finally, any nonzero polynomial in Q[q] has degree at least 0. Our quotient is nonzero and has negative degree, so it cannot belong to Q[q].

Thus, if 0<=a<b<=n/2, the rational function [n choose a]_q/[n choose b]_q has negative degree and therefore is not an element of Q[q].
role_in_parent: After symmetry reduction, this forces the reduced numerator index to be at least the reduced denominator index.
statement_nl: For integers n, a, b with 0 <= a, b <= n, define [n choose t]_q := prod_{i=1}^t (1 - q^(n-t+i)) / (1 - q^i), with the empty product equal to 1 when t = 0. Then the degree in q of [n choose a]_q is a(n-a). Consequently, if 0 <= a < b <= n/2, then the rational function [n choose a]_q / [n choose b]_q has negative degree and therefore does not belong to the polynomial ring Q[q].

domain_restrictions: implicitly n >= 0 (since 0 <= a,b <= n is required)
in the degree claim, [n choose a]_q is formed with t=a (so a is used as the product upper limit)
in the ratio claim, 0 <= a < b <= n/2 (with n/2 interpreted numerically; b is integer so effectively b <= floor(n/2))
statement_semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For all integers n,a,b with 0 <= a,b <= n: define the Gaussian binomial coefficient [n choose t]_q = ∏_{i=1}^t (1 - q^(n-t+i)) / (1 - q^i), with the empty product for t=0 equal to 1. Then deg_q([n choose a]_q) = a(n-a). Moreover, for all integers n,a,b with 0 <= a < b <= n/2, the rational function [n choose a]_q / [n choose b]_q has negative degree (i.e., deg_q([n choose a]_q) - deg_q([n choose b]_q) < 0), hence [n choose a]_q / [n choose b]_q is not an element of Q[q].
quantifier_order: for any t used in the definition (implicitly t in Z with 0<=t<=n when specializing)

variables.name: n
variables.role: upper parameter controlling both the Gaussian binomial coefficient and the domain 0 <= a,b <= n

variables.name: a
variables.role: exponent/parameter in [n choose a]_q; left index for the degree computation and numerator of the ratio

variables.name: b
variables.role: right index for the denominator of the ratio and for the inequality 0 <= a < b <= n/2

variables.name: t
variables.role: dummy index used in the definition of [n choose t]_q; satisfies 0 <= t <= n when used to instantiate [n choose a]_q or [n choose b]_q

variables.name: q
variables.role: variable with respect to which degrees are taken; defines rational function coefficients over Q
